tip: से glues onto pronouns: उस + से = उससे (usse = than that one). यह कमरा उससे ठंडा है – the 'than that' is one small fused word.
बेहतर (behtar = better), from Persian, is one of Hindi's few true comparative words: पुराने वाले से बेहतर = better than the old one. Most adjectives rely on से alone.
For people, बड़ा (bada = big) means older: मुझसे दो साल बड़ा (mujhse do saal bada) = two years older than me. छोटा (chhota = small) likewise means younger.
'As well as' uses a pair: उतना ही अच्छा... जितना (utna hi achchha... jitna) = 'that much good... as much as'. Hindi spells out both halves of the match.
तेज़ (tez) covers fast, sharp, and strong: याददाश्त तेज़ (yaaddaasht tez) = a sharp memory, तेज़ चाकू = a sharp knife, तेज़ धूप = strong sun.
Verb + ने वाला makes 'the ...-ing kind': भरने वाला (bharne vala) = filling, literally 'the one that fills'. Works on nearly any verb.
This से is 'from', not 'than': छठी कक्षा से (chhathi kaksha se) = from sixth grade onward. से does both jobs; हो जाता है (ho jata hai = becomes) signals a starting point here.
Verb stem + कर = 'after ...ing': खाना खाकर (khana khakar) = after eating. Two syllables replace a whole English clause – 'having eaten, she washes up'.
Liking flips: मुझे चाय पसंद है (mujhe chai pasand hai) = 'to me tea is pleasing'. The liker takes मुझे/को (mujhe/ko = to me/to); the tea is the subject.
के हिसाब से (ke hisaab se) = 'by the account of' = according to: राजेश के हिसाब से = according to Rajesh. हिसाब (hisaab) means account or calculation.
Vehicles drink fuel: कम पेट्रोल पीती है (kam petrol peeti hai) = uses less petrol, literally 'drinks less'. पीना (peena) also covers smoking – सिगरेट पीना.
साबूदाने की खिचड़ी (sabudane ki khichdi = sago khichdi) is the classic व्रत (vrat = fast) meal – grains are avoided on fasting days, and sago isn't a grain.
Doubling a word spreads it out: अलग-अलग (alag-alag = different-different) = all kinds of. Hindi repeats where English says 'various' or 'each'.
With हमने (humne = we), the verb agrees with the thing made: बनाई (banai) is feminine because रोटी (roti) is – 'made' matches the roti, not us.
There is no word for cousin – you describe the route: मामा का बेटा (mama ka beta) = mother's brother's son. Cousins are often simply called भाई (bhai = brother).
करोड़ों (karodon = crores of): Hindi counts big numbers as लाख (lakh = 100,000) and करोड़ (crore = 10 million) – 'million' barely exists in daily speech.
मेहनत रंग लाई (mehnat rang layi) = 'the hard work brought color' – the set idiom for effort paying off. In Hindi, success shows up as color.
ही (hi) stresses the word before it: होती ही हैं (hoti hi hain) = simply ARE longer. This tiny word does what English does with voice stress or 'indeed'.
'Best in the area' becomes 'the area's best': इलाके का सबसे अच्छा डॉक्टर (ilake ka sabse achchha doctor) – Hindi reaches for का (ka = of) where English says 'in'.
बनते हैं (bante hain) = 'get made': बनना (banna) is a verb meaning 'to be made', so लड्डू बनते हैं says laddoos get made with no doer mentioned.
से can compare against an idea: उम्मीद से ज़्यादा (ummeed se zyada) = 'more than hope' = more than expected. Any noun can serve as the measuring stick.
किया करते थे (kiya karte the) adds 'made a habit of it' – the verb's -या (-ya) form + करना (karna) is a step more nostalgic than plain करते थे (karte the). Common when reminiscing.
One respected grandmother, plural verb: दादी (dadi) takes सुनाती थीं (sunati theen), not थी (thi). Elders and parents get grammatical plural as respect.
गाकर (gaakar = having sung) – adding -कर (-kar) to a verb means 'by/after doing it', chaining actions with no word for 'and': sang, and so put us to sleep.
'Played chess well' – well is the adjective अच्छी (achchhi), agreeing with feminine शतरंज (shatranj). Manner words often match the object's gender.
English 'play' splits in Hindi: instruments take बजाना (bajana = make sound) – बाँसुरी बजाता था (bansuri bajata tha). Games take खेलना (khelna). Never swap them.
मीठा होता था (meetha hota tha) = 'used to be sweet, as a rule'. Plain था (tha) would pin it to one occasion – होता था signals a general truth back then.
जाता था (jata tha), the -ता (-ta) form + था (tha), is Hindi's plain 'used to' – no extra word needed. पहले (pahle = earlier) just sets the scene.
साइकिल से (saikil se) = by bike – से (se) is the all-purpose 'by/with/from': vehicles, tools, and starting points all use the same little word.
काग़ज़ की नावें (kagaz ki naavein) = boats of paper – की/का (ki/ka) marks material, and it agrees with the thing made: feminine की for the boats, not the paper.
